items.title: Why AI Agents Need a New Data Stack
items.summary: Deepti Srivastava on AI Agents, Live Data, and the Return of Federation. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Deepti Srivastava , founder and CEO of Snow Leopard , joins us to discuss why AI agents need access to live enterprise data and why traditional approaches to data integration may not be enough. We explore how AI is making data federation and automatic semantic layer construction more practical, and the challenges of accuracy, governance, and reliability. We also discuss why MCP alone isn’t enough, the tradeoffs between federation, warehousing, and streaming, and what the data stack might look like in an agent-first world. Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have my friend Deepti Srivastava, founder and CEO of Snow Leopard, which you can find at Snow Leopard AI. The tagline is “Empower Your AI Agents with Live, Accurate Data in Minutes.” Snow Leopard, with its automatic semantic data intelligence, provides 90-plus percent data accuracy out of the box, so you can ship enterprise agents faster and with confidence. And with that, Deepti, welcome back to the podcast. Deepti Srivastava. Thank you, Ben. It’s super exciting to be back here. Ben Lorica. All right. So I guess the thesis is agents need data. In fact, agents need the right data at the right time. I think that makes sense. I think a lot of our listeners will agree with this. So agents need data, and data, for the most part, will have to be retrieved. I think that also makes sense, right? So right now, I guess the current state of Snow Leopard is that it sits between your databases and the agents that need information from them. An agent sends a question through an API, and then Snow Leopard works out which database holds the answer, writes the queries, fetches the results, and combines them. Deepti Srivastava. That’s correct. Yes. Ben Lorica. And the emphasis here, Deepti, am I right to say the emphasis is on operational data, not analytic data like data warehouses? Deepti Srivastava. The emphasis is on operational data. I think analytics data can also be used as part of operational data. But the way I think about this is operational data sits in structured storage, right? So structured storage is SQL databases, APIs like Salesforce or HubSpot, or things like that, right? Things that make your business run or are part of critical business decision-making. So, for example, there is a lot of data that is unstructured. And overall, if you remember back to 2023, 2024, and 2025, even RAG was all the rage for unstructured data, right? Because it was the first time that we could actually assemble and make sense of unstructured data. But really, the focus from Snow Leopard’s side, from my side, has always been operational data that makes your business run. So it’s stuff that is in SQL Server or Postgres or MySQL or Snowflake, which can be both analytical and, you know, people use it for operational data today as well. So things like that, and Neon, and SOQL from Salesforce, because they’ve become critical to how you run your business. And they are therefore critical to how you will run autonomous agents, right? Because the whole point is we not only automate current workflows, but we create new workflows with the power of Gen AI, to be specific, right? And so autonomous agents, AI agents, are meant to be that unlocking force. And for them to work, they need, like you said, access to the right data from the right place at the right time. So if it is a warehouse, we’ll talk to the warehouse. Ben Lorica. So basically, the focus of Snow Leopard, so to speak, is data in databases. So it could be operational, it could be analytic, and then databases that use SQL. Is that another assumption, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes. Ben Lorica. So then, one of the things that you do is, let’s set aside how you write the SQL statement for now. But one of the things you do is, let’s say I’m an AI agent that’s interacting with an external customer. Based on the inferred need of the customer, you will decide where the data lives. It could live in multiple places. Write the SQL and then return to the customer what the customer needs. So implicit in this, I think lurking in the background, is a dirty word called federation. Am I wrong? Deepti Srivastava. No, you’re absolutely right. I don’t think of it as a dirty word, but yes, it is. Absolutely. Ben Lorica. Federation has had a long history, right? Ben Lorica. So let’s have you play devil’s advocate first. Why are people skeptical of federation? Deepti Srivastava. Because historically it hasn’t worked, right? Historically, the way to do federation has been… Ben Lorica. By the way, maybe you should give a very high-level definition of federation. Deepti Srivastava. Federation means you go to different data sources and fetch data from them. Whether it’s live or not is a separate question. But the point is, you have some data in one database, some data in another database. So Postgres and MySQL used to be the canonical examples. And then you don’t know how to get data from both of them, right? Your customer data can be in Postgres, your product usage data can be in MySQL, for example, or the other way around, right? And so the question becomes, how do you combine that information in order to answer a question, even if it was for a dashboard, right? Even if it was historical trend analysis, you still have to go get data from both. And so the overall thought process over the past 20 years was that you use an ORM and then you use base SQL, right? The common ANSI SQL standard of the time. And then you write every query in that form so that your LAMP-stack-type application would then go fetch from, you know, the program would basically write the SQL query in the base SQL language, and so it could run anywhere, right? Because the idea was that it was standardized SQL, so it could run anywhere. And so you could write basic SQL and get data from, let’s say, MySQL and Postgres, right? Because both of them would support basic SELECTs and basic JOINs. But what’s implicit or explicit in that is that the basic feature functionality set becomes the lowest common denominator. You actually can’t use most of the functionality that each database provides completely, right? So it becomes this hobbled-together system, and you have to have exceptions all over the place in order to really use the MySQL stuff versus the Postgres stuff versus the Teradata stuff versus the Oracle stuff. So that doesn’t work. Also, federation used to be really hard because you couldn’t figure out a priori, which is how most software has been built until now. Right? Pre-agent, all software is built a priori, which means all the logic has to be pre-programmed. Which means you don’t know which data silo you have to go to in order to get that information a priori. So putting together federation became practically really, really hard, if not impossible. Which is where this concept, which, by the way, I agree with in the pre-AI world, this concept of warehousing became so popular. Because now you dump everything into a warehouse. The warehouse is known in its boundaries, and now you can write your program very deterministically in order to get information from the warehouse. Ben Lorica. But that’s only good for analytics and reports. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. So the current warehouse vendors will argue with you that real-time pipelining and sub-minute blah, blah, blah will give you that, but it doesn’t. And all of your listeners who’ve ever done this know that it’s not true, right? So you use the analytic-style capabilities to run sort of real-time-ish workloads. Ben Lorica. There’s always going to be a lag, right? Deepti Srivastava. There’s always going to be a lag. And the problem is, at human speed, this was still okay because we would fill in the gaps ourselves, right? I think this is the biggest thing that people are now facing in real time. They’re realizing as they build autonomous agents that some of that lag, when the human was the operator, we could fill in, right? We could go look up Salesforce and give you an answer if you’re sitting in a boardroom. Or the customer support example that you’re saying: the human customer support agent can go look at the data source if they have access, right, and give you an answer like, “Where is my order?” even if it hasn’t made it to the warehouse. I think the difference today is, and it’s a really important difference, that an autonomous agent, if it doesn’t have access to the right information, cannot give you that information, right? So a lot of support calls today, I’ve done this even recently, if your e-commerce workflow fails at the wrong time, where your user calls in and says, “I didn’t get my order number, so I don’t know if the order went through or not,” which is the canonical example I give because I faced it. So you’re going to talk to a chatbot. The chatbot’s going to ask you for your order number. You do not have your order number. Then it has to transfer you to the human to bridge that last 30% gap where it doesn’t have the information, right? And now, if you have autonomous decision-making agents, like how much marketing spend to have, right? Which microtransaction in financial services to actually let go? Those things, you cannot intervene, right? Ben Lorica. But still, why does federation work now? Deepti Srivastava. Two things. In the era of Gen AI, we can actually, and this is known, write text-to-SQL on the fly, right? And because of Gen AI, if you actually work with it with an understanding of how systems and databases work, you can do live federation across systems by making real-time decisions that you previously couldn’t without Gen AI, right? So that’s actually what the premise of Snow Leopard is. This is possible now because LLMs can do text-to-SQL at a base level, right? And we can make decisions based on live pattern matching, if you will, which LLMs are very good at. So you don’t have to have if-then-else conditions for every single thing that is out there. And that’s why it works. Ben Lorica. So then, in the example you gave, right, you have customer data in Postgres and product data in MySQL. First of all, I think one of the things you do when you engage with someone is you understand the schema across all these databases, right? So then, I guess, what people call the semantic layer, right? Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Ben Lorica. So a lot of people have this. Sometimes they have it only for their system. There are some BI tools that have it across different analytic systems, right? So if you use Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, they’ll have it. But you’re building it across these operational systems, right? So then that means you understand that the customer data is in Postgres, the product data is in MySQL, but then you still have to do JOINs potentially, right? Deepti Srivastava. And we can do that outside those systems. That is the key sort of insight or value-add of Snow Leopard, that we can JOIN across those data sources. Ben Lorica. And the reason is because the types of queries you’re working with are not going to be these massive, big queries like, here’s a billion-row table, JOIN it with this, right? So they’re operational systems, right? Deepti Srivastava. So there are two parts to that answer, right? The first part is yes. I think everybody that’s in the data space goes into, like, “Oh my God, but the worst-case scenario…” Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Which is actually why federation also didn’t work earlier, right? Side note: I literally recently wrote a research article for the ACM about what’s required for data architectures. I’ll send you a link to it because it talks about what was wrong with federation in more detail and why it works now in more detail. But the point is, we can build these semantics a priori, first of all, at connection time. And we can use that at query time to write the SQL, right? So that’s one part of the system. But to go back to your question of why this will work and how come we won’t go into the pathological case, I think data shows operational data queries are generally, generally speaking, point lookups or small JOINs, right? So when we talk about this customer example, it’s one customer making 10 orders, maybe, right? So those are not the pathological cases. So yes, we work really well. In fact, if you demo it, if you use it yourself, we can answer these questions in real time, very, very quickly, right? Because we are doing all this stuff with point lookups and point JOINs, and we can parallelize and distribute and put the information together very quickly. So that’s one thing. The second thing is, any data person that has worked with databases, etc., knows there are known optimization techniques, right? So, for example, if we see JOINs that are large, we can break them down, first of all, right? We can optimize the query. The databases themselves do that. Secondarily, if we have had to do it once, we can cache it. There are multiple techniques. There’s caching, there’s subquery generation. You can do a MapReduce kind of thing with queries, right, where you can break them up, pull the data in separately, and then put it back together. This is what we did at Oracle for large JOINs and batch JOINs and things like that. You can create views and things like that. So there are multiple ways in which we already know how to optimize that part that we can apply. And these are known and solved problems, so it’s a matter of application. The hardest part is what Snow Leopard is solving today, which is: Where is my data? How do I connect it? How do I get the right context so that the text-to-SQL is highly, highly accurate? How do we get governance, right, so that the agent doesn’t touch the wrong data? And how do we actually use these SQL databases with the agents? Where the answer today is, “Oh, just MCP it.” And I think we’re finally coming out of the trough of disillusionment around MCP. The last time we talked, it had just come out, and there was this whole hype that MCP will solve everything. It doesn’t solve governance. It doesn’t solve accuracy, right? It actually burns a lot of tokens. So all of these things that are practical issues that you and I know are hard, right? Data is one of those things where you can say, “Oh, I know how to solve it,” but the devil is in the details. And you spend 90% of your time trying to deal with the edge cases, outliers, and things like that, which become very common, right? Those are the hard parts. Ben Lorica. So the semantic layer, right? This is key to what you do. You go into a company, and then in order for you to do your magic, you have to infer automatically this kind of semantic layer. Correct? Semantic layer broadly defined, basically understanding what data is available, where it is, and what the right permissions are, and so on and so forth, right? But key is, you know, this column, which might be called, I don’t know, 12345, is actually customer ID, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes. Ben Lorica. Right. So how well does that automatic construction of the semantic layer work out of the box? Deepti Srivastava. So we ran a benchmark against Sonnet 5.6, the latest versions of Opus, and the latest GPT version at the time, like four months ago. These things move really fast. But we were 90-plus percent accurate, 95-plus percent accurate in our benchmark. And we didn’t shenanigan it. We literally just ran Snow Leopard with the datasets, which were BigQuery and Postgres, and public datasets. We didn’t shenanigan the dataset either. And these LLMs plus MCP, right? And we didn’t do just 10 questions, right? We ran 100 questions three times. There is a benchmark that we published. So number one, we do really well. Ben Lorica. By the way, operational data tends to live in these really ginormous schemas, right? So thousands of tables potentially, right? ERP systems are a mess, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes, I think all of that is true. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Again, I think if you look at the sum total of all the databases that people have been trying to use with autonomous systems today, there’s a bell curve, right? The meat of the bell curve is maybe 5,000 schemas, right? That kind of thing. And those are very simple. The way we’ve built the system is that it is scalable, right? So it doesn’t get trapped with, “We have 10 terabytes of data,” because we don’t care. The schemas are large, yes. But I think I want to go back to what it means to build semantic intelligence, right? What does it mean to have a semantic layer? Because people focus a lot on ontology definition on one end of the spectrum and schema reading on the other. And Snow Leopard is built on the premise that you need both and more, right? So I think in order to have semantic intelligence, you have to understand not just the schemas, but also the system from which you are reading those schemas. So SQL Server is very different from Postgres, which is very different from MySQL, which is very different from BigQuery, from Snowflake, etc. And I’m not even getting into SQL, right? But each of these databases has a way in which you define the schema and the data. So the way Snow Leopard works is, first of all, we have AI harnesses that are custom to that database type, which means we understand that BigQuery has schemas a certain way. Names, for example, are put differently in BigQuery versus Postgres versus MySQL. MySQL has schemas. Postgres has namespaces and datasets. BigQuery has only datasets, right? So step one for accuracy is you have to know what the layout is going to look like, right? Step two is, yes, we read the schemas, but any fool can read the schemas at this point, right? So that is not it. We read the schemas, but we actually have an LLM-based harness with judges and adversarial LLMs or systems that actually probe the data within the schemas. Which is how we know that column 12345 has floating-point decimals and therefore must be a currency column or a discount column or things like that, right? Versus it has whole numbers and they’re five digits, so therefore it might be ZIP codes. Ben Lorica. Right, right. Deepti Srivastava. Right. This is how we build that intelligence, and we do all of this at the time you connect the data source. So that’s number one. That’s how we get accuracy out of the box. And the number two piece is we completely agree that tribal knowledge today exists in people’s heads. And so we actually provide you with an interface to then give feedback. We literally call it the feedback API to the system, to Snow Leopard, so that you can say, “Oh, actually, you thought column ABCDE was a discount number, but it’s actually our price reduction number,” right? Ben Lorica. This is actually key. Your API is quite simple, right? So you have the response, you have retrieve response, and then this feedback, right? And the feedback allows you to go from 95% to more and more accuracy, right? Deepti Srivastava. Correct. Yes. Ben Lorica. And actually, this is interesting because one of the books I read recently, which I really like, is called Everywhere Millionaires . And it’s really about two academic economists who, after grad school, went to the U.S. Treasury Department, and they were trying to understand small businesses. And they got stuck trying to understand it until one of them gave a talk somewhere in Utah and ran across the guy who built the system. And all of the understanding around it, and the whole book and their entire research agenda, flowed out of this guy explaining to one of them what these tables are, because it’s just not documented, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes. So this is my concern about things like catalogs and ontologies. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Because once you document it, it becomes stale. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. And it’s always fragmented. Ben Lorica. Right. Deepti Srivastava. Right. And so those are great as starting points, but in order to understand the system, you actually need to know what the live, beating system looks like, right? So we do automatic schema detection, drift detection, and then update semantics, as an example, right? These are little things, but they are so difficult to deal with and require so much manual work, even today. Ben Lorica. So in defense of the rest of the industry, you’re not the only one trying to do this kind of automatic semantic detection, semantic layer construction, ontology construction using AI, right? So have you paid attention to what others are doing, and where do you think you shine in this? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. To be honest with you, I really don’t think people are treating it as a holistic problem. Snow Leopard is built on the fact that we need a new data architecture, a new data stack for AI. Ben Lorica. Well, for one thing, you’re not a data management provider, so you’re not assuming that everything we just mentioned, semantic layer construction, ontology construction, is limited to your data management layer. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. So we pull out from being part of any one data management system because that data management system is very optimized for them, right? And they don’t care about all the other systems out there. Ben Lorica. And the reality is, most big companies use many different systems. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Data silos are a fact of life, right? And so number one is that. Number two is we’re actually looking at it as a holistic problem. So not just ontology and automated semantics generation, but also upkeep and maintenance. So we have three pillars, right? We have automated context, which is automated semantic intelligence, automatic and live federation, and governance. And on top of all of these is ease of use. So we care really a lot about, most of the people on your podcast probably have this problem, how do we make the lives of people who are managing these systems easier? So to your point about competitive analysis or landscape, people focus on just the ontology or just the schema reading or just the semantic layer overall, right? Build a graph database and you’ll have a semantic layer. Use this ontology system and you’ll have ontology, right? But you need more than that. DBT has a great way for you to do metrics. Google has a similar one to define ontology, to define metrics, to define pipelines. But you have to do the work, right? With Snow Leopard, the approach is we’ll do all the work that we can and then allow you to tweak where you need to. That’s number one. Number two, there’s going to be another system that will federate. I don’t think any system is federating right now, by the way. I’ve looked many times. Unless there’s a verticalized solution where they’re selling you a solution, right? An analytic solution. Most people in this space are selling an analytic solution. We are selling a platform on which you can build your own analytic solution, and you can build your own agent of any kind, right? And so the third thing is governance, which then becomes a third solution. So the main point is, you as the end user or the builder have to pick multiple different solutions in order to build the full end-to-end application you want. And with Snow Leopard, we’re trying to make most of that something that you don’t have to deal with. Like, pick this vendor for governance, and this vendor for MCP, and this vendor for semantics, and this vendor for federation. Ben Lorica. So this is a hard question to answer. But how much of this unwritten business knowledge can an AI reasonably infer? I guess that’s why you have this feedback API. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Yeah. So we started with no human feedback required, and then I very quickly got to SAP HANA and SQL Server and Salesforce, which are not that easy to read, right? And so, yes. Ben Lorica. So this feedback API. Let’s say I provide you this feedback, right? There are two departments, and they define active customers differently, but actually Department A’s definition is more accurate. So then I give you that feedback. How quickly does the system adjust? Deepti Srivastava. Within a few minutes. Ben Lorica. Okay. Deepti Srivastava. So again, just because you’ve given me feedback, or Snowy feedback, doesn’t mean we’re going to take it, right? So we have a whole verification and analysis and judgment layer in the feedback system that will actually look at where it applies, whether it makes sense or not, and then we’ll apply it, right? And then we apply it immediately to your session, and then we see how the session is going, right? And then based on that, we will bake it into the system. So we are very careful because we don’t want bad actors to change definitions, obviously. But we can take it and absorb it in real time. So the thing you gave me, just to pinpoint that, like you said, Department A’s definition is different, let’s say, from Department B’s. Whether it’s accurate or not, the system doesn’t know. But we can actually say this is Department A that’s talking to the same system, right? To the same set of data sources. Ben Lorica. Well, because you know based on my role. Deepti Srivastava. Correct. And so we can actually apply it for you and not apply it for the other one. So the technical solution here is we layer semantics. Ben Lorica. But what if I assert that actually it’s universally understood by the rest of the company, except for Company B, that my definition is the correct one? Deepti Srivastava. You mean Team B, right? Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. And then that’s fine. If it’s Team B, again, we have roles. So if it’s somebody from Team B asking the question, or using the agent, or the agent is assuming the role of Team B, we can answer that way versus not, right? Ben Lorica. So 95% accuracy sounds great, but that 5% might break my business. If I’m 5% inaccurate, it might drive my customers away. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think there’s two answers. Ben Lorica. So then you have this feedback mechanism, right? Deepti Srivastava. But I think, Ben, the answer is… Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Let’s be realistic. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. What are you getting today out of the box? Ben Lorica. Yeah, right. Deepti Srivastava. Like for anybody that’s doing this, right? If you just connect and go, which is what we’re promising with Snow Leopard, is connect and go, right? The idea is, again, you can see how far the system can get, and then you can give feedback on it, right? That is the point. And you can do acceptance of the system as the administrator. We give you the tools to do the acceptance on your own, but without having to build everything, right? And so no probabilistic system is going to give you 100% determinism out of the box. Our aim is to marry these probabilistic engines with deterministic outcomes, reaching as close to 100% as possible. Even humans make mistakes, right? So obviously we’re not promising anything that is foolproof or bulletproof, but we’re trying to make it as close to that as possible. And I think today it’s even more possible with LLMs and Gen AI than it used to be, even three years ago, even when we started two years ago. Ben Lorica. So then, now I have, let’s say I deploy Snow Leopard, right? So now I have my agents having access to the right data at the right time. But now I have a single point of failure, which is Snow Leopard. If Snow Leopard goes down, I’m screwed. So what do you say to listeners who say, “Well, I’m going to wait until Deepti and company have more of a track record. I know that this is hardened,” and so on and so forth, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think nothing I say will make somebody change their mind about what risk they are able to take or want to take. I will say, try it, right? And the other thing is, we have been working with financial services companies that have been using us. And so I think the point is, we work with you. Yes, we are an early-stage company, but we work with you in order to get you to have the kind of reliability you want, right? And then because our solution is BYOC, we can be inside your cloud. We can be on our own cloud, right? So we aim to be the strongest link in your chain. Because clearly, with data, there is a chain, and there are weak links and strong links. I want us to be the stronger link in the chain, not the weak one. Ben Lorica. So what are some of the DevOps numbers that people want to know, right? Uptime, latency. Latency depends on the source system to a large extent, right? Deepti Srivastava. So we do not… Ben Lorica. Concurrency, right? So what if you can only support two users at a time? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I don’t think that’s the case, right? Because we are, from the ground up, built to be cloud-resilient. And so we have high concurrency. We can support hundreds of users at the same time. The on-prem deployment, again, concurrency is a function of how much resources you give to it, right? And so the on-prem deployment, we can parallelize. We have built the system to be parallelizable and highly efficient from the ground up, right? We are a bunch of systems engineers and AI engineers to start, so we’ve built it that way. I think in terms of latency, we add some microseconds, if at all, to those responses. We are faster, by the way, 10x faster than MCP directly. Ben Lorica. And you don’t burn all these tokens, right? Deepti Srivastava. And we use half the tokens. Yeah, I was going to say that. We’re 10x faster than MCP and use half the tokens on average. Again, it depends on what you’re doing, but we’re at half the tokens on average. Ben Lorica. But also, you have this federation, which is key to, I think, making a lot of agents useful moving forward, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes, I truly believe that without having federation in some format, people will not be able to use autonomous agents for critical workflows, right? Because you really do need to have access to the right systems. Ben Lorica. Since you’ve made federation respectable, I have to point out that Databricks, who I am an advisor to, has also made another thing respectable, which is, what is it called, the hybrid transactional analytic systems, right? So unifying OLAP and OLTP. So let’s set that aside. It works well, but you have to be in the Databricks world, right? So another approach besides unifying transactional analytic storage is, I guess, streaming. Are people trying to do this with streaming? Deepti Srivastava. I think they’re trying to. From the people I speak to… Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. I spoke to a head of data and AI in MarTech. It’s the second-largest MarTech firm in the U.S., and they were like, “It just doesn’t work,” right? For them, for a lot of use cases, because… Ben Lorica. So maybe explain to our listeners what we mean by streaming in this context. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. So the idea is going back to Kafka and the pre-AI world. I think all of this is pre-AI world, pre-Gen-AI world, to be specific, where consolidation was the only way to do a bunch of things because we hated federation for various reasons. And so one of the things was you stream data out of databases and into a warehouse or into a lake. And in the stream, you can do a bunch of cool things like attach SQL on top of the stream. So you could make queries happen for dashboards or things like that, right? And then you have faster streaming or broader streaming, so you can have multiple databases that are pushing to the same data warehouse or lake. And then you can do transformation in those streams so that you can basically have views on this data in motion, so you can make faster decisions than you could with only the warehouse, right? Ben Lorica. So how does this help me? How does this help me in the context of an agent trying to look up something like an order? Deepti Srivastava. To be honest with you, I don’t know, because how reliable is the stream? So you’re doing a bunch of manual work. And for those people who are doing a bunch of manual work to build functionality around these streams, maybe it works for them for specific use cases, right? I think the point I’m trying to make is… Ben Lorica. But it’s very hard. Every use case, you have to do it. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. It’s custom. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. It’s brittle. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. And if any column was added to the source table, now you have to change the stream because streams have definitions, to add that and then put it in the warehouse. Ben Lorica. Well, I have an AI to do the semantic layer for the stream. Deepti Srivastava. Yes, yes. And to not have to… I think the point is, people started using streaming as the way to query because putting it in the warehouse was taking too long. So this is again another way to say near real time, near real time. It’s not real time. And also, you define streams for specific workflows. Data pipelines are designed to be specific. So if you try to use a data pipeline or a data stream for everything at all times, it’s going to break because it’s like a round peg, square hole situation, right? So the way to build applications on top of streams became a way to do fresher data, right? To not have staleness because it’s stale by the time it gets to the warehouse. But the other problem with that is it’s transformed, and so you’ve lost meaning in the pipeline because you had designed that pipeline to be for analytics, for example, for historical trend analysis, for example. So you’ve made the columns and rows picked specifically for that use case, right? And so now you don’t have the full picture. So if you’re going to put something that is a decision-making agent on top of that stream, it’s not going to have the full picture. It’s going to give you wrong answers, just point-blank, right? Ben Lorica. So what I like about what you do is this: you’re not making copies of the data, right? So you’re hitting the data where you need it, and then you make the reasonable assumption that, hey, data is not going to be conveniently located in one system. It’s going to be located in multiple systems, and I need the freshest data, so I don’t want that data to be copied first before I hit it. All of that is well and good, but obviously one thing that people have been reading about is this agents-going-rogue scenario, right? So now I have a scenario where these agents can interact with an application that’s hitting my live systems and making all sorts of potentially nefarious requests. So I guess you alluded to this earlier. You have the notion of governance and all of that. What are some of the things you can say to reassure listeners that this doesn’t open up their systems to rogue agents? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I will say, if you’re using MCP today, you’re already open to rogue systems, right? Because MCP by definition, on its own, is just like HTTP, right? It doesn’t have any of that governance built in. So I actually feel scared when people are using MCP on top of their databases, right? Because once you have MCP, there are just two APIs, right? So all it does is it has access to all of your data and all of your schema unless you do custom work inside the MCP or on top of the MCP, right? So again, now we’ve gone to custom work. So just as a rule, I think by itself MCP doesn’t help you solve this problem. Then people, as I was saying earlier, vendors sell governance on top of MCP or governance-built MCPs, right, that you then have to configure. So with Snow Leopard, the point is, because we sit outside of all of your data sources, in between your agent and your data sources, we can actually be that person, sorry, the system in the middle that can arbitrate. I can route things to different places, and only when it’s allowed. So one of the things I talk about in this ACM article is governance on not just roles and access control, but who and why. Because an agent can impersonate. In fact, that’s how most agents work today. You impersonate somebody else’s role. Ben Lorica. I mean, people are going to start using agents like Muse and Dots, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. I mean, the thought is scarier without governance. And so the point is, because we sit outside the systems, when an agent makes a call, the agent itself can tell us, and needs to tell us, who it is and what it’s trying to do, right? Team A versus Team B in your earlier example. And based on that, we can federate. Maybe Team A only has access to… Ben Lorica. What about if I’m a Muse agent acting on behalf of Ben? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, same thing, right? Because again, if Muse has to interact with Snow Leopard and you, there are two things happening, right? One is Snow Leopard knows it’s Muse and therefore has access to Ben’s credit cards, but maybe not a direct bank account and direct Zelle. And so we will not let Muse do that. Number one. So what that means is we arbitrate where you are going to go, or we have the ability to arbitrate where you’re going to go based on who is asking the question, which agent, and on behalf of whom. Second is, you can actually set up Snow Leopard to have access to only a certain set of data to begin with, right? And because it’s just a matter of connect and go with Snow Leopard, you can just add or remove not just datasets and data sources, but tables. So, for example, you can give Snow Leopard access today to one of your, let’s say, BigQuery datasets and some of the tables in that BigQuery dataset, right? So we use a combination of existing database access control as well as agent-based access control of what are they trying to do, and how and why are they trying to do it, and then push that down to get the right information, right? So because this stuff is outside, even if Ben has access to all of your financial systems, maybe the agent Muse does not. And so we can enforce that because we’re sitting outside. Ben Lorica. So as I opened this podcast, I thought I used the word retrieval, so that implies read-only, correct? So do you think that there will be a future where Snow Leopard can update these databases, or never? Deepti Srivastava. 100%, yes, we can. It’s just a matter of giving read access versus write access. I think right now, based on where the world is at, read itself is hard enough and scary enough. Ben Lorica. It’s scary enough, yeah. Deepti Srivastava. I think the scary part is more important. Like SELECT versus UPDATE are just permissions, honestly, to a database. The way I think about it, right, a database is just about whether you can do SELECT statements or whether you can do UPDATE statements. And right now, we are not allowing Snow Leopard to do UPDATE statements, but we can. It’s just a bit set. Again, these things are known. I just don’t think there is enough trust in touching, not trust in Snow Leopard, but just trust in AI and autonomous agents in general. And we can. This is just a technology problem, and that’s very easy to solve. I think the trust problem is a different problem. Ben Lorica. So this is probably something that is outside your system. It’s more of a question for security teams, right? But when an agent uses Snow Leopard to retrieve information across these systems, whose permissions is it using? Deepti Srivastava. Right now, the permissions are either granted through a service account or through a role that Snow Leopard is given access to. So, for example, for BigQuery, we use OAuth and SSO, and so then it becomes whoever the user is, right? But if you set up a service account, then we can use the service account, right? So it’s up to the user administrator, really, to set up the right security roles right now. And I don’t think the security problem is solved. I think what I’m excited about for us is that we’ve built the system in a way that we can actually add on to security and governance practices as they evolve for agents, right? Because again, we are not tied to one system, so we don’t have to have, “If you are in this world, then you can do this, otherwise not,” right? We are very easily evolvable. I believe in evolution because AI agents and autonomous agents themselves are evolving, and so I believe in evolving the system to that. And I think the way we’ve set it up, there’s a lot of room for us to evolve as the industry evolves. Ben Lorica. So this semantic layer construction, automatic semantic layer construction, it seems like… Do you think most companies have systems in place where, when you come in and you try to infer their data, the semantic layer automatically, do you think their systems are well-architected enough so that, out of the box, this semantic layer is reasonable? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, sorry, I… Ben Lorica. Because the reason I ask is there’s these teams in companies. One of the most awful jobs in these companies is this thing called master data management. Have you heard? Deepti Srivastava. Yes. Ben Lorica. Right. So it’s like a lot of people doing all of these things manually, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yes. Ben Lorica. And so then, to me, that implies that maybe their underlying systems are a mess. So if their underlying systems are a mess, then how well will this automatic inferring of the semantic layer work, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think this is a common refrain from people who are on the data side of the world, right? From people who are trying to build on the agent side of the world, they’re like, “Just give me something, because right now I have nothing,” right? So yes, data is a mess. I think it’s messier than most people think it is. But also, there’s a lot more we can do. It is surprising even to us what we can do with the harnesses and the way we’ve built them for Snow Leopard, right? So we can actually get a long way through. And this is why we added feedback, because whatever the last mile is, nobody is guaranteeing that the data will not be messy. I think there are two things. One, getting started is the hardest part with this data, because if you’re going to have a two-year-long project to move everything onto… Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Deepti Srivastava. …the system of choice. Ben Lorica. So you guys come in, you infer the semantic layer, and then I assume the first set of users are people in the IT group. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, the administrators. Ben Lorica. Yeah, so then they’re trying to give you feedback before they deploy, right? Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. And the thing is, you can continue to adjust very easily, because the APIs for the agents are very simple, and the user interfaces for human beings are also very simple, right? So if IT approves something for the marketing department, the marketing department can then go off and fine-tune it. The other problem with these master data management jobs is that there are few people trying to address the needs of the entire company, right? So if you can set it up so that each team at least can use something without you having to worry about it, and without you having a huge queue of work for each of those systems, I think that’s a huge unlock for the company overall, right? And then the other thing is, I want to bring it back down to, yes, data is messy, but we can go a long way with that without too much human intervention. And then you can add the human intervention to tweak, which is a time saver versus starting from scratch. Second, you can allow, because of the way the APIs and the feedback are set up, even people who are not in the IT department to give feedback in order to adjust semantics, etc., right? So you’re not constantly going back to the IT department. Very quickly, I’ll give you an example. Again, this fintech company we worked with, we worked with the founding engineer who was also basically the head of data, managing all of this stuff. And he could reduce his workload because he could just point people to the Snow Leopard-based agent to answer a bunch of questions instead of him having to build DBT pipelines and then write the SQL and then iterate over the SQL and then give them the answer, and then having to do that for every team and every question all the time. Ben Lorica. As I understand it, you have some sort of tool for explainability, right? So in other words, when I first deploy you and I’m in the IT team, not only am I giving you feedback, there’s a certain level of explainability. So I’m reassured that, okay, it’s hitting the right systems, it’s writing the right SQL. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Yes. And that built-in explainability is right in front of you. So if you look, the API returns it, by the way, so that even if you build autonomous agents, agents can verify, if you put the verification loops in there. By the way, we have APIs for both the agents and the humans. The humans can see, this is on our website too, the SQL being generated, the data sources being targeted, and the reason how and why we built it. So it’s natural language explanations of the SQL query we built and why we built it, right? So you’re talking to your agent, or your agent is talking to Snow Leopard, and it can see what happened. So you can say, “Oh, it built SQL with this table and this column, but actually it needs to use this other table and this other column for this specific question on churn or on profit,” right? Because these can be very, very ambiguous terms, as you said, different for different people. Ben Lorica. So what feedback have you gotten about this explainability tool? Is it good enough, or do you have plans to tweak it and improve it? Deepti Srivastava. Both. We have gotten feedback that it’s better than what they’ve seen, so they’re excited about it because they didn’t even know that you could get this kind of detailed information. And then the common one I get is, “Can you draw it as a picture, essentially? Can you build an ER diagram?” Ben Lorica. Right. Deepti Srivastava. Right. And I think that’s like, or a graph or something that says, “We went here, we went here, we went here.” So that’s something we are considering adding. We can also do it custom, especially for messy data or for large teams. It makes more sense to just visualize it very quickly, especially the ontology part of it, the semantic layer part of it, because it is hidden. And a lot of data people are like, “I don’t like hidden.” So showing it in a visual format is something we’re considering for sure. But I want to know feedback. And if people are more interested in having it one way or the other from your audience, I would love that. So please let me know. Ben Lorica. So if someone makes an adjustment to the schema or gives you feedback, and therefore you have to make an adjustment, so some adjustment is made, right? Can you go back in time and understand, okay, so if we showed Ben this last week, but we should have shown him this in light of what we know now? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, that’s a good question. So we have auditability because, again, I come from the data world. I don’t like it if I don’t know what the steps were. So yes, we have auditability where you can see, even today in the cloud product, we have some auditability where you can say, “This person gave this feedback, and it was applied to this database,” right? And once it’s applied, it means it’s there right now. Do we explain or have the whole stack exposed? I think we have it exposed to us in the back end from a debuggability perspective, from a DevOps perspective. I don’t think we show all of that in the front end. But again, we are early. We’re very open to feedback on how people would want to see it. But again, we’ve built the system because I know our people want to see more and more and more, and have more transparency. Ben Lorica. So Snow Leopard is basically all about SQL databases and data in SQL databases. Any plans for other types of data? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. It’s not just SQL databases anymore. It’s Salesforce as well, which is SOQL, which is API, and graph databases are not SQL. So we will add as many connectors as we need based on the customers. So far, we’ve had mostly folks who want to connect or JOIN across one of these databases, right? SQL databases, and Salesforce seems to be the most popular API. But we are absolutely set up for APIs as well, structured APIs, not blob APIs. Ben Lorica. Never unstructured data? Deepti Srivastava. I just think there’s a whole body of work and research and vendors out there that are doing that. I think this is a hard problem. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. And I have expertise in this. I just want to solve this problem. Ben Lorica. So if you look three years ahead, what will the data stack look like? Obviously, Snow Leopard is right there. Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think the data stack needs to have agents, a data… This is another bad word. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. Middleware. But data middleware, right? And then the data sources at the end, right? So one of the things that I didn’t say earlier is, we are not saying no to warehouses. If the data exists in the warehouse, we can go get it from the warehouse too. Really, it’s just a question of where is the data. And if you have a RAG vector store, basically for RAG pipelines, we can query from that too. That’s not a big deal either. I think the point is, federation is key because you need to know where the data is and how to get it from there, right? So I imagine the stack having governance as a pillar, where the governance is around both the data as well as the agents. So not just what, but who and why are one of the key pillars for the data stack for AI agents. The other is just federation has to be key, and so it needs to be really, really easy. It cannot be consolidating everything into one place. I just don’t think that works. I mean, I’m not saying what Databricks or Snowflake are doing is not great. I think it is, but not everybody’s data everywhere is in one place. And so federation has to be key, live federation. And then the third thing is this machine-readable, automatic understanding of the business context, which we call the semantic layer. But really, it’s automatic understanding of the business logic, which has to be a part of it, with human feedback, whatever form that takes, right? Regardless of Snow Leopard, I think these three are the key pillars in order to make autonomous decision-making agents work. Ben Lorica. And by the way, if agents actually start writing more code, there’s no reason why they wouldn’t write code for the data teams and the data engineering teams. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Ben Lorica. So which means, actually, the data stack itself will change constantly because maybe, you know, now you’re coding, you’re using coding agents. “Oh, let’s rebuild the schema in the database tomorrow,” right? So fire up agents next week. We have a completely different schema and whatever, right? Or we never used this piece of infrastructure because we didn’t have in-house expertise. Now we can use it. Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Ben Lorica. So then people might be constantly making adjustments to their data infrastructure, which means this middleware might actually be super important, right? I think as long as the middleware constantly infers all these changes, right? Deepti Srivastava. But this is my point to you. I think a lot of the concerns that you brought up, which I hear, these are legitimate concerns, are from a world where humans are curating carefully all of this stuff, right? But we are going to an agent-first world, right? Some of us are already there. Others are getting there, right? Ben Lorica. In a world where people are throwing away code. Deepti Srivastava. That’s my point. Even in an agent-first world, it does not matter what the pipeline is, what the code is, because it’s going to change every time. And so that’s why we have automatic semantics and automatic schema drift detection, right? Because we have to actually update based on what the agents are doing, right? So if the agent is changing the data underneath you, you didn’t even know what it was doing, right? Because you care about outcomes. Muse is about outcomes, for example, right? And so to your point, if everything is changing, the middleware has to understand that something changed, semantics changed, context for getting data from the right place has changed. And so all of this just has to be automatic at machine speeds, not human speeds, and with enough verification, where governance comes in, right? So I think the agent-first world requires us to be in this three-pillar system, right? For data especially. And yes, we will get there in time. So we do need to have human interfaces, but agent-first means agent interface, agent speeds, machine-readable stuff, and not worrying about everything always being hand-curated because it cannot be. Ben Lorica. And static, right? Because I guess the world I’m imagining is these data teams who will become bolder and move faster, and they will throw away pieces of their infrastructure more quickly. And then you need this kind of Snow Leopard layer so that your agents can access the data as the data team is constantly ripping out and replacing things underneath you, right? Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, and you have to be efficient with that, right? Ben Lorica. Yeah. Deepti Srivastava. So I think static is a great word. I just don’t think we are going to go from a static world to a dynamic world. We’re already going there. If we believe agents are going to create and undo databases as a result of whatever work they have to do, or as part of whatever work they have to do, then these things become all automated, right? The middleware has to exist and has to have strong boundaries and automation in order to enable the data teams to do that. Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Deepti. And you can learn more by visiting Snow Leopard AI. Deepti Srivastava. Thank you, Ben.

Deepti Srivastava on AI Agents, Live Data, and the Return of Federation.

Deepti Srivastava, founder and CEO of Snow Leopard, joins us to discuss why AI agents need access to live enterprise data and why traditional approaches to data integration may not be enough. We explore how AI is making data federation and automatic semantic layer construction more practical, and the challenges of accuracy, governance, and reliability. We also discuss why MCP alone isn’t enough, the tradeoffs between federation, warehousing, and streaming, and what the data stack might look like in an agent-first world.

Transcript

Below is a polished and edited transcript.

Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have my friend Deepti Srivastava, founder and CEO of Snow Leopard, which you can find at Snow Leopard AI. The tagline is “Empower Your AI Agents with Live, Accurate Data in Minutes.” Snow Leopard, with its automatic semantic data intelligence, provides 90-plus percent data accuracy out of the box, so you can ship enterprise agents faster and with confidence. And with that, Deepti, welcome back to the podcast.

Deepti Srivastava. Thank you, Ben. It’s super exciting to be back here.

Ben Lorica. All right. So I guess the thesis is agents need data. In fact, agents need the right data at the right time. I think that makes sense. I think a lot of our listeners will agree with this. So agents need data, and data, for the most part, will have to be retrieved. I think that also makes sense, right? So right now, I guess the current state of Snow Leopard is that it sits between your databases and the agents that need information from them. An agent sends a question through an API, and then Snow Leopard works out which database holds the answer, writes the queries, fetches the results, and combines them.

Deepti Srivastava. That’s correct. Yes.

Ben Lorica. And the emphasis here, Deepti, am I right to say the emphasis is on operational data, not analytic data like data warehouses?

Deepti Srivastava. The emphasis is on operational data. I think analytics data can also be used as part of operational data. But the way I think about this is operational data sits in structured storage, right? So structured storage is SQL databases, APIs like Salesforce or HubSpot, or things like that, right? Things that make your business run or are part of critical business decision-making.

So, for example, there is a lot of data that is unstructured. And overall, if you remember back to 2023, 2024, and 2025, even RAG was all the rage for unstructured data, right? Because it was the first time that we could actually assemble and make sense of unstructured data.

But really, the focus from Snow Leopard’s side, from my side, has always been operational data that makes your business run. So it’s stuff that is in SQL Server or Postgres or MySQL or Snowflake, which can be both analytical and, you know, people use it for operational data today as well. So things like that, and Neon, and SOQL from Salesforce, because they’ve become critical to how you run your business. And they are therefore critical to how you will run autonomous agents, right?

Because the whole point is we not only automate current workflows, but we create new workflows with the power of Gen AI, to be specific, right? And so autonomous agents, AI agents, are meant to be that unlocking force.

And for them to work, they need, like you said, access to the right data from the right place at the right time. So if it is a warehouse, we’ll talk to the warehouse.

Ben Lorica. So basically, the focus of Snow Leopard, so to speak, is data in databases. So it could be operational, it could be analytic, and then databases that use SQL. Is that another assumption, right?

Deepti Srivastava. Yes.

Ben Lorica. So then, one of the things that you do is, let’s set aside how you write the SQL statement for now. But one of the things you do is, let’s say I’m an AI agent that’s interacting with an external customer. Based on the inferred need of the customer, you will decide where the data lives. It could live in multiple places. Write the SQL and then return to the customer what the customer needs.

So implicit in this, I think lurking in the background, is a dirty word called federation. Am I wrong?

Deepti Srivastava. No, you’re absolutely right. I don’t think of it as a dirty word, but yes, it is. Absolutely.

Ben Lorica. Federation has had a long history, right?

Ben Lorica. So let’s have you play devil’s advocate first. Why are people skeptical of federation?

Deepti Srivastava. Because historically it hasn’t worked, right? Historically, the way to do federation has been…

Ben Lorica. By the way, maybe you should give a very high-level definition of federation.

Deepti Srivastava. Federation means you go to different data sources and fetch data from them. Whether it’s live or not is a separate question. But the point is, you have some data in one database, some data in another database. So Postgres and MySQL used to be the canonical examples.

And then you don’t know how to get data from both of them, right? Your customer data can be in Postgres, your product usage data can be in MySQL, for example, or the other way around, right? And so the question becomes, how do you combine that information in order to answer a question, even if it was for a dashboard, right? Even if it was historical trend analysis, you still have to go get data from both.

And so the overall thought process over the past 20 years was that you use an ORM and then you use base SQL, right? The common ANSI SQL standard of the time. And then you write every query in that form so that your LAMP-stack-type application would then go fetch from, you know, the program would basically write the SQL query in the base SQL language, and so it could run anywhere, right?

Because the idea was that it was standardized SQL, so it could run anywhere. And so you could write basic SQL and get data from, let’s say, MySQL and Postgres, right? Because both of them would support basic SELECTs and basic JOINs.

But what’s implicit or explicit in that is that the basic feature functionality set becomes the lowest common denominator. You actually can’t use most of the functionality that each database provides completely, right? So it becomes this hobbled-together system, and you have to have exceptions all over the place in order to really use the MySQL stuff versus the Postgres stuff versus the Teradata stuff versus the Oracle stuff. So that doesn’t work.

Also, federation used to be really hard because you couldn’t figure out a priori, which is how most software has been built until now. Right? Pre-agent, all software is built a priori, which means all the logic has to be pre-programmed. Which means you don’t know which data silo you have to go to in order to get that information a priori.

The way I think about it, right, a database is just about whether you can do SELECT statements or whether you can do UPDATE statements.

And right now, we are not allowing Snow Leopard to do UPDATE statements, but we can. It’s just a bit set.

Again, these things are known. I just don’t think there is enough trust in touching, not trust in Snow Leopard, but just trust in AI and autonomous agents in general.

And we can. This is just a technology problem, and that’s very easy to solve. I think the trust problem is a different problem.

Ben Lorica. So this is probably something that is outside your system. It’s more of a question for security teams, right?

But when an agent uses Snow Leopard to retrieve information across these systems, whose permissions is it using?

Deepti Srivastava. Right now, the permissions are either granted through a service account or through a role that Snow Leopard is given access to.

So, for example, for BigQuery, we use OAuth and SSO, and so then it becomes whoever the user is, right?

But if you set up a service account, then we can use the service account, right?

So it’s up to the user administrator, really, to set up the right security roles right now.

And I don’t think the security problem is solved.

I think what I’m excited about for us is that we’ve built the system in a way that we can actually add on to security and governance practices as they evolve for agents, right?

Because again, we are not tied to one system, so we don’t have to have, “If you are in this world, then you can do this, otherwise not,” right?

We are very easily evolvable.

I believe in evolution because AI agents and autonomous agents themselves are evolving, and so I believe in evolving the system to that.

And I think the way we’ve set it up, there’s a lot of room for us to evolve as the industry evolves.

Ben Lorica. So this semantic layer construction, automatic semantic layer construction, it seems like…

Do you think most companies have systems in place where, when you come in and you try to infer their data, the semantic layer automatically, do you think their systems are well-architected enough so that, out of the box, this semantic layer is reasonable?

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, sorry, I…

Ben Lorica. Because the reason I ask is there’s these teams in companies. One of the most awful jobs in these companies is this thing called master data management. Have you heard?

Deepti Srivastava. Yes.

Ben Lorica. Right. So it’s like a lot of people doing all of these things manually, right?

Deepti Srivastava. Yes.

Ben Lorica. And so then, to me, that implies that maybe their underlying systems are a mess.

So if their underlying systems are a mess, then how well will this automatic inferring of the semantic layer work, right?

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think this is a common refrain from people who are on the data side of the world, right?

From people who are trying to build on the agent side of the world, they’re like, “Just give me something, because right now I have nothing,” right?

So yes, data is a mess. I think it’s messier than most people think it is.

But also, there’s a lot more we can do. It is surprising even to us what we can do with the harnesses and the way we’ve built them for Snow Leopard, right?

So we can actually get a long way through.

And this is why we added feedback, because whatever the last mile is, nobody is guaranteeing that the data will not be messy.

I think there are two things. One, getting started is the hardest part with this data, because if you’re going to have a two-year-long project to move everything onto…

Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Deepti Srivastava. …the system of choice.

Ben Lorica. So you guys come in, you infer the semantic layer, and then I assume the first set of users are people in the IT group.

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, the administrators.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, so then they’re trying to give you feedback before they deploy, right?

Deepti Srivastava. That’s right.

And the thing is, you can continue to adjust very easily, because the APIs for the agents are very simple, and the user interfaces for human beings are also very simple, right?

So if IT approves something for the marketing department, the marketing department can then go off and fine-tune it.

The other problem with these master data management jobs is that there are few people trying to address the needs of the entire company, right?

So if you can set it up so that each team at least can use something without you having to worry about it, and without you having a huge queue of work for each of those systems, I think that’s a huge unlock for the company overall, right?

And then the other thing is, I want to bring it back down to, yes, data is messy, but we can go a long way with that without too much human intervention.

And then you can add the human intervention to tweak, which is a time saver versus starting from scratch.

Second, you can allow, because of the way the APIs and the feedback are set up, even people who are not in the IT department to give feedback in order to adjust semantics, etc., right?

So you’re not constantly going back to the IT department.

Very quickly, I’ll give you an example. Again, this fintech company we worked with, we worked with the founding engineer who was also basically the head of data, managing all of this stuff.

And he could reduce his workload because he could just point people to the Snow Leopard-based agent to answer a bunch of questions instead of him having to build DBT pipelines and then write the SQL and then iterate over the SQL and then give them the answer, and then having to do that for every team and every question all the time.

Ben Lorica. As I understand it, you have some sort of tool for explainability, right?

So in other words, when I first deploy you and I’m in the IT team, not only am I giving you feedback, there’s a certain level of explainability.

So I’m reassured that, okay, it’s hitting the right systems, it’s writing the right SQL.

Deepti Srivastava. That’s right. Yes.

And that built-in explainability is right in front of you.

So if you look, the API returns it, by the way, so that even if you build autonomous agents, agents can verify, if you put the verification loops in there.

By the way, we have APIs for both the agents and the humans.

The humans can see, this is on our website too, the SQL being generated, the data sources being targeted, and the reason how and why we built it.

So it’s natural language explanations of the SQL query we built and why we built it, right?

So you’re talking to your agent, or your agent is talking to Snow Leopard, and it can see what happened.

So you can say, “Oh, it built SQL with this table and this column, but actually it needs to use this other table and this other column for this specific question on churn or on profit,” right?

Because these can be very, very ambiguous terms, as you said, different for different people.

Ben Lorica. So what feedback have you gotten about this explainability tool? Is it good enough, or do you have plans to tweak it and improve it?

Deepti Srivastava. Both.

We have gotten feedback that it’s better than what they’ve seen, so they’re excited about it because they didn’t even know that you could get this kind of detailed information.

And then the common one I get is, “Can you draw it as a picture, essentially? Can you build an ER diagram?”

Ben Lorica. Right.

Deepti Srivastava. Right. And I think that’s like, or a graph or something that says, “We went here, we went here, we went here.”

So that’s something we are considering adding.

We can also do it custom, especially for messy data or for large teams. It makes more sense to just visualize it very quickly, especially the ontology part of it, the semantic layer part of it, because it is hidden.

And a lot of data people are like, “I don’t like hidden.”

So showing it in a visual format is something we’re considering for sure.

But I want to know feedback. And if people are more interested in having it one way or the other from your audience, I would love that. So please let me know.

Ben Lorica. So if someone makes an adjustment to the schema or gives you feedback, and therefore you have to make an adjustment, so some adjustment is made, right?

Can you go back in time and understand, okay, so if we showed Ben this last week, but we should have shown him this in light of what we know now?

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, that’s a good question.

So we have auditability because, again, I come from the data world. I don’t like it if I don’t know what the steps were.

So yes, we have auditability where you can see, even today in the cloud product, we have some auditability where you can say, “This person gave this feedback, and it was applied to this database,” right?

And once it’s applied, it means it’s there right now.

Do we explain or have the whole stack exposed? I think we have it exposed to us in the back end from a debuggability perspective, from a DevOps perspective.

I don’t think we show all of that in the front end.

But again, we are early. We’re very open to feedback on how people would want to see it.

But again, we’ve built the system because I know our people want to see more and more and more, and have more transparency.

Ben Lorica. So Snow Leopard is basically all about SQL databases and data in SQL databases. Any plans for other types of data?

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah. It’s not just SQL databases anymore.

It’s Salesforce as well, which is SOQL, which is API, and graph databases are not SQL.

So we will add as many connectors as we need based on the customers.

So far, we’ve had mostly folks who want to connect or JOIN across one of these databases, right? SQL databases, and Salesforce seems to be the most popular API.

But we are absolutely set up for APIs as well, structured APIs, not blob APIs.

Ben Lorica. Never unstructured data?

Deepti Srivastava. I just think there’s a whole body of work and research and vendors out there that are doing that.

I think this is a hard problem.

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Deepti Srivastava. And I have expertise in this. I just want to solve this problem.

Ben Lorica. So if you look three years ahead, what will the data stack look like? Obviously, Snow Leopard is right there.

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, I think the data stack needs to have agents, a data… This is another bad word.

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Deepti Srivastava. Middleware. But data middleware, right? And then the data sources at the end, right?

So one of the things that I didn’t say earlier is, we are not saying no to warehouses.

If the data exists in the warehouse, we can go get it from the warehouse too.

Really, it’s just a question of where is the data.

And if you have a RAG vector store, basically for RAG pipelines, we can query from that too. That’s not a big deal either.

I think the point is, federation is key because you need to know where the data is and how to get it from there, right?

So I imagine the stack having governance as a pillar, where the governance is around both the data as well as the agents.

So not just what, but who and why are one of the key pillars for the data stack for AI agents.

The other is just federation has to be key, and so it needs to be really, really easy.

It cannot be consolidating everything into one place. I just don’t think that works.

I mean, I’m not saying what Databricks or Snowflake are doing is not great. I think it is, but not everybody’s data everywhere is in one place.

And so federation has to be key, live federation.

And then the third thing is this machine-readable, automatic understanding of the business context, which we call the semantic layer.

But really, it’s automatic understanding of the business logic, which has to be a part of it, with human feedback, whatever form that takes, right?

Regardless of Snow Leopard, I think these three are the key pillars in order to make autonomous decision-making agents work.

Ben Lorica. And by the way, if agents actually start writing more code, there’s no reason why they wouldn’t write code for the data teams and the data engineering teams.

Deepti Srivastava. That’s right.

Ben Lorica. So which means, actually, the data stack itself will change constantly because maybe, you know, now you’re coding, you’re using coding agents.

“Oh, let’s rebuild the schema in the database tomorrow,” right?

So fire up agents next week. We have a completely different schema and whatever, right?

Or we never used this piece of infrastructure because we didn’t have in-house expertise. Now we can use it.

Deepti Srivastava. That’s right.

Ben Lorica. So then people might be constantly making adjustments to their data infrastructure, which means this middleware might actually be super important, right?

I think as long as the middleware constantly infers all these changes, right?

Deepti Srivastava. But this is my point to you.

I think a lot of the concerns that you brought up, which I hear, these are legitimate concerns, are from a world where humans are curating carefully all of this stuff, right?

But we are going to an agent-first world, right? Some of us are already there. Others are getting there, right?

Ben Lorica. In a world where people are throwing away code.

Deepti Srivastava. That’s my point.

Even in an agent-first world, it does not matter what the pipeline is, what the code is, because it’s going to change every time.

And so that’s why we have automatic semantics and automatic schema drift detection, right?

Because we have to actually update based on what the agents are doing, right?

So if the agent is changing the data underneath you, you didn’t even know what it was doing, right? Because you care about outcomes.

Muse is about outcomes, for example, right?

And so to your point, if everything is changing, the middleware has to understand that something changed, semantics changed, context for getting data from the right place has changed.

And so all of this just has to be automatic at machine speeds, not human speeds, and with enough verification, where governance comes in, right?

So I think the agent-first world requires us to be in this three-pillar system, right? For data especially.

And yes, we will get there in time.

So we do need to have human interfaces, but agent-first means agent interface, agent speeds, machine-readable stuff, and not worrying about everything always being hand-curated because it cannot be.

Ben Lorica. And static, right?

Because I guess the world I’m imagining is these data teams who will become bolder and move faster, and they will throw away pieces of their infrastructure more quickly.

And then you need this kind of Snow Leopard layer so that your agents can access the data as the data team is constantly ripping out and replacing things underneath you, right?

Deepti Srivastava. Yeah, and you have to be efficient with that, right?

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Deepti Srivastava. So I think static is a great word.

I just don’t think we are going to go from a static world to a dynamic world. We’re already going there.

If we believe agents are going to create and undo databases as a result of whatever work they have to do, or as part of whatever work they have to do, then these things become all automated, right?

The middleware has to exist and has to have strong boundaries and automation in order to enable the data teams to do that.

Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Deepti. And you can learn more by visiting Snow Leopard AI.

Deepti Srivastava. Thank you, Ben.

items.title: How to Choose a Compute Platform Your Products Won't Outgrow - with Kyle Larson of IDEMIA
items.summary: As AI accelerates software development, the hardware that software runs on is still often built on a slower, separate track, and the gap shows up in what customers receive. In this episode, Kyle Larson, VP of AI Enablement and Cloud Services at IDEMIA, examines why hardware and software now need to be planned and delivered as one product. He covers how to decide what runs on the device versus in the cloud, why developer tools and simulation need to be in place before physical prototypes arrive, and how to evaluate a long-term compute platform by the ecosystem and supplier roadmap around it.
